title: Mitred square — basic
subtitle: A flat square built by decreasing from a corner rather than growing from the centre
excerpt: The mitred square starts at a corner cast-on and works inward through a central decrease on every right-side row, landing on a single stitch at the opposite corner. Two triangular halves meet at the diagonal spine, giving a neat seam line that reads as a design detail in stripe colourwork.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1887), mitred and diagonal squares chapter (Internet Archive). Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) documents the mitred construction; the crochet equivalent follows the same geometry.
heroPrompt: A basic mitred crochet square in warm oatmeal DK cotton on a pale linen background, photographed flat from above in soft daylight. The diagonal spine runs corner to corner across the 10 cm square, perfectly flat.

crochet.gaugeText: Each finished mitred square measures 10 × 10 cm in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook, after a light steam-block.

chartDefinition.title: Mitred square — basic
chartDefinition.caption: The chart reads from the top corner downward. Each row is one stitch shorter than the last; the central dc2tog on every row creates the diagonal spine.

glossaryTerms.definition: Double crochet two together: insert hook, pull up a loop, insert hook in next stitch, pull up a loop, yarn over and draw through all three loops. Decreases by one stitch.
The diagonal decrease line that runs from corner to corner through the centre of a mitred square, created by working dc2tog at the midpoint of every row.

content.text: The mitred square builds from a corner chain downward, shrinking by two stitches on every row through a central decrease on the diagonal. This construction is the opposite of the granny square: instead of growing outward from a ring, the mitred square collapses inward from its widest edge to a single stitch at the tip.

attrs.title: Materials for one motif
attrs.body: About 8 g of DK-weight cotton. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle and scissors. One stitch marker to track the centre decrease point.

content.text: Each finished mitred square measures 10 × 10 cm in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook, after a light steam-block. The final stitch count per row depends on your starting chain count; adjust the foundation chain in multiples of 2 plus 1 for a larger or smaller square.
double crochet (dc) — UK; US single crochet.
Worked in rows, turning at each end. Ch 1 at the start of each row does not count as a stitch.
Dc in 2nd ch from hook and in next 8 ch. Place a stitch marker in the next ch. Work
over marked ch and following ch. Dc in each remaining 9 ch. Turn. (19 sts.)
Ch 1. Dc across to 1 st before centre marked st. Move marker to centre st of this row. Dc2tog over next 2 sts. Dc to end. Turn. (2 sts decreased per row.)
Ch 1. Dc2tog over remaining 2 sts. Fasten off. (1 st.)

definition.title: Mitred square — basic
definition.caption: Rows run from top corner downward. Central dc2tog on every row creates the diagonal spine.

content.text: Fasten off and weave in both ends along the edge rows. Steam-block by pinning the square to a blocking mat at the corners, holding steam 2 cm above for 10 seconds, and leaving to cool flat.
Whip-stitch through back loops along any two edges for a flat seam. For a chevron layout, rotate alternate squares 180 degrees so the diagonal spines meet in a zigzag.

Work the two-colour mitred square next, joining a contrast yarn at the start of the decrease rows to make the diagonal spine a feature stripe. For a larger surface, the log cabin square uses the same row-based approach.
